Documentation

The person who knew how everything worked has left, and now every question stops at an empty chair. We write the knowledge down, decisions and reasons included, with one named owner keeping it current.
The empty chair problem

When what your team knows, and why big decisions were made, lives in one person's head, that person's last day is where the work stalls. Docs that exist but belong to nobody quietly stop being true after a few changes.

Then something breaks and the blame starts circling, because nothing was written down at the start. We've seen a client caught between several contractors, each pointing at the next, for exactly that reason.

We're Roxana Negaresh and Arshia Amani, and we treat documentation like a product. First an audit: what exists, what's missing, what's plain wrong. Then each document gets an audience, a format, an update rule and an owner, and your own team reviews it before handover. We don't write from thin air, either: documentation without a source is just a guess. The scope template we sign before every project is public, if you'd like to see what we count as a good document: dadmor’s real project scope template.
Who needs this most

items: Your product or API has to be usable by customers or outside developers without them asking you.
You're handing a project from one team or contractor to another.
You want the why behind technical decisions on record, not only the what.

blocks.html: Where we'd stop you

items: The document would sit in a folder and nobody would ever open it.
We can't get access to the system, the code, or the people who know it. Without a source, documentation is guesswork.
You need legal writing: contracts, terms of use, a formal privacy policy. That's a lawyer's work, not ours.

blocks.html: What we actually write
How the writing runs

items: Audit. Input: your existing documents, access to the system, and time with the key people. Output: an honest list of what exists, what's missing and what's wrong. Owner: dadmor.
Structure. Input: the audit. Output: a document list, each item with its audience, format, update rule and owner. Owner: dadmor; approval: you.
Write. Input: the structure you approved, and access to the sources. Output: the documents themselves, reviewed by one person from your team. Owner: dadmor; technical review: you.
Handover. Input: the approved documents. Output: everything in its final home, plus a session on how to keep it updated. Owner: dadmor.

blocks.html: What changes the workload

items: What sets the size: how many documents, how many API endpoints, whether you need both languages, and how reachable the sources are, code and people alike.
From you: access to the system and code, time from the key people, and one technical reviewer.
What delays it: a key person who never has time to talk, and a system that keeps changing while it's being documented.

blocks.html: Rough size

items: Every phase is proposed separately, at a fixed price. You can order just the audit.

blocks.html: This band is a starting estimate, and it depends on the state your documents are in now. We settle it after the scoping conversation, once we've seen them.
What paper can't do

items: A document stays right only while somebody follows its update rule. After handover, that's the owner named in the structure.
Legal text isn't ours to write.
We only publish samples of your documents with your permission, and redacted.
